newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Philippines fends off Thai financial epidemic.
newsitem.headline: Philippines fends off Thai financial epidemic.

text.p: The Philippines pounced on speculators on Thursday, hoping to prevent the financial troubles in Thailand from spreading to its own markets, but not all analysts were convinced it would work.
The Central bank raised interest rates twice during the day and dumped more than $70 million in the morning to protect the peso.
"The increase (in rates) might trigger selling again in the stock market. This is just another excuse to sell," Asia Capital Equities analyst Jonathan Ravlas said.
But as the Central Bank, which raised overnight interest rates by a hefty 1.75 basis points in one day, had some succcess in propping up a weakening peso, share prices tumbled.
The Manila share market index plunged almost three percent to 2,631.09, and now stands about 17 percent below its level at the start of April.
The initial slide in April came after fears that the Philippines was about to copy Thailand's property and banking crisis.
On Thursday, traders again blamed Thailand where the baht came under strong attack on fears about the health of its economy.
"It's all contagion from Thailand...We're very vulnerable. The reason is we have a history to live down," Luz Lorenzo, economist with Peregrine Securities, said.
The government insists that after five years of consistent growth the bad old days in mismanagement and boom-bust cycles are over.

Finance Secretary Roberto de Ocampo pointed to latest figures which showed the government's budget surplus, at 18.2 billion pesos ($692 million) in the first four months of the year, were above expectations.

"Improving macro fundamentals are expected to contribute to a stronger growth performance in the months ahead...This latest information belies unfounded rumours that the Philippines is going Thailand's way,' he said.

But analysts said Manila still had to prove itself to the investor community which is already looking jaded about the fortunes of southeast Asia at a time when the Philippines is only just beginning to catch up.
"There should be some concrete antidote to cure the situation," Angping and Associates Securities managing director, Wilfred Son Keng Po, said.
He was looking for approval of the government's final tax reform package, which is currently making slow headway through Congress.
Tax reform is linked to the end of more than 30 years of International Monetary Fund supervision, and for the Philippines a crucial step in its ambition to become another Asian Tiger.
The key, in the short-term, for its financial markets is likely to be economic growth figures for the first quarter which are due to be announced later this month.
"I want (the gross domestic product) figure to be more than five percent. If it touches four percent it will trigger somne sell-offs," Son Keng Po said.
